- Chooses to stress-test the strongest case (catching an AI red-handed trying to escape) as an extreme thought experiment, because if even that evidence fails to persuade, weaker evidence like model organisms or interpretability will do worse.
- Chooses what to study partly by how well it prepares for the possibly enormous impacts of future, more capable systems, not only by present-day benchmarks.
- Prefers running evaluations in a secure environment without real useful-work affordances over deployment-like access, because the eval doesn't need dangerous affordances.
- Distrusts extrapolating from non-analogous settings and from sandwiching-style results, since models may sabotage them; wants explicit accounting for the possibility that the model is gaming the evaluation.
- Test for subtle side channels that let a model infer it is being paused, rerun, or in a different inference setup, rather than assuming it can't tell.
- prefers testing realistic, topic-specific or goal-directed behaviour over blanket instructed behaviour because the realistic threat does not look like the simple lab elicitation.
- Splits evaluation data into artifact-solvable (Easy) and artifact-resistant (Hard) subsets to see how much of the measured success depends on surface cues.
- Distrusts results from iterating and evaluating on the same problem set, flagging overfitting risk and the need for held-out validation.
- Prefers naturally-occurring distributions over hand-built ones where viable because they reduce the risk that the benchmark is skewed in ways that omit important phenomena, though acknowledges they are often not viable.
- Distrusts results framed to deemphasize system successes as a reaction to hype, since the framing reflects a social motive and not the evidence.
- prefers making offers to the model real and following through on them over merely fictional promises because credible, honest dealings set a precedent and make the model's responses to the scenario more meaningful.
- Prefers evaluations built on easy-to-measure capability assumptions over ones that depend on hard-to-test properties, because the latter let developers make flawed or cherry-picked safety arguments from weak, illegible evidence.
- Hunts for adversarial examples where relatively natural-looking inputs cause weird behavior, i.e. realistic-seeming inputs rather than obviously contrived ones.
- prefers testing with a blind/ablated baseline that cannot access the intended signal over trusting headline benchmark scores because success may come from shortcuts rather than the target capability.
- Sees the model's ability to tell the real deployment context apart from fakes (e.g. the date and observations being forgeable, or conditioning on features of a real AI-company deployment) as the key axis along which test scenarios fail to elicit defection.
- Prefers evidence from naturally arising behavior in a setup closely resembling the real training or deployment over engineered prompts, and requires that the malign behavior not rely on extra knowledge the model couldn't plausibly have.
- Frames results modestly as toy demonstrations that offer a foundation for further study, not as direct evidence about real-world deceptive behavior.
- Future work should test how conclusions change with evaluators of varying capability and with other feedback forms, and evaluate oversight techniques on misleading errors.
- Concerned with how capabilities or knowledge given to an AI for alignment can raise its power faster than its alignment, so safety interventions must be tested for side effects.
- Uses simple statistical analysis (PMI of words with labels, length distributions) to surface which lexical cues give away the label.
- Frames capability gaps such as situational awareness and planning as what stands between current models and undetectable sabotage, so these are the capabilities worth tracking.
- Flags as an open research topic finding better evidence for why current models are not scheming than informal impressions of their answers.
- Uses qualitative transcript review and participants' own notes alongside accuracy numbers to understand what strategies work and where trust breaks down.
- Prefers cautious interpretation of noisy measurement instruments over taking them at face value, flagging that confidence labels are not true probabilities because the incentive scheme is not proper.
- Verifies the model actually has the capability or knowledge before counting a failure as a behavioral one, so the failure can't be attributed to ignorance.
- Open problem: formalizing the evaluation for recursive/multi-agent oversight setups and handling capability elicitation failures like exploration hacking.
- Prefers testing safety against a red-team attack policy that actively exploits the protocol's weaknesses over testing with the honest model's behavior, because safety must hold even when the model is intentionally subverting.
result:
- Unlike peers, grades evidence on a realism ladder (capability exists, special circumstances, normal training, robustness to anti-training), so evidence strength depends on how much unrealistic steering was needed.
- Unlike peers, starts with maximal spoonfeeding and removes it progressively, treating the remaining steering as a measure of how far a failure mode is from arising naturally.
- Unlike peers, requires causal intervention on the chain of thought to confirm that the dangerous behavior is downstream of the reasoning step, and does not treat the scratchpad alone as evidence of true motives.
- Unlike peers, filters generated fine-tuning data to keep only samples that verifiably exhibit the target behavior, rather than assuming the behavior is present.
- Unlike peers, delivers situational facts through fine-tuning on synthetic pretraining-like documents rather than the system prompt, removing salient in-prompt cues.
- Unlike peers, probes for hidden behavior with conditional framings, such as offering a chance to come clean or switching the audience from outsiders to in-group, because deception may surface only when incentives appear to change.
- Unlike peers, builds honeypots where revealing a hidden goal is the model's optimal move, while acknowledging that real auditors lack this prior knowledge of the goal.
- Unlike peers, holds out more natural model organisms as a test set rather than iterating on every artificial one, because repeated iteration on the same examples risks overfitting.
